summary: A fragment of a fiction piece in which Robbie, a robot rowing a boat at sunset, rescues divers floating among lifeless colorful sea creatures. He hauls in a passive 'human-shell' he calls Isaac, then realizes the diver he calls Janet is a real, panicking human and helps her aboard using his oar. The passage touches on Asimov's robot laws and the limits of Isaac's programming.
one_line: A robot named Robbie rescues divers at sunset, discovering that one he took for a human-shell is a real, panicking woman.
key_facts: Robbie is a robot rowing a boat with servo-driven oars at sunset.
Robbie calls the human-shell man 'Isaac'; he hauls himself into the boat with his strong brown arms.
Human-shells are uninhabited bodies that float with their BCDs inflated, following perfect dive procedure.
Waves of up to a meter and a half in length were pounding the divers and knocking them under.
The woman Robbie calls Janet climbs along his oar and cries 'Get me out! for Christ's sake, get me out!'
Robbie realizes Janet is a live human, not a human-shell, and tips up his oar-servo to lift her.
Weight belt, tank and gear pull Janet down while she is half in, half out of the water.
Isaac sits motionless with a good-natured slight smile; it isn't in his programming to help a fellow diver in the boat, so he is like ballast.
Robbie pleads 'for Asimov's sake' and recalls the first commandment: a robot may not harm a human or, through inaction, allow one to come to harm.
Robbie switches on his running lights and headlights to become a beacon after the sun fully sets.
Janet chins herself into the boat and collapses on the deck; the air turns nippy and both humans get goose pimples.
The reef makes a grinding noise and says 'Yaah! Get lost. Sovereign territory!'
A stray line says Gary mentioned that he has been vegan for years.
